sections.html:
Bracken County is small and entirely rural, laid out along the Ohio River in northern Kentucky. Brooksville holds the courthouse, Augusta is the biggest town, and Germantown is the third incorporated city. The 2025 estimate is 8,511 residents, and the county sits inside the Cincinnati metro area.

Housing is inexpensive. The typical owner's home is valued at $125,000, and owners live in 78.5% of homes. Typical rent is $756 a month, and a mortgaged owner pays about $1,144 a month. The 2020 count found 3,839 housing units, 13.3 percent of them empty. Few residents move (95.7 percent stayed in the same house for a year), and the average trip to work is 34.5 minutes. When a value dispute comes up, the sales records kept at the PVA are what the county appeals board looks at.

sections.h2: Who to call about a Bracken County tax bill
sections.html:
Valuing and collecting happen in separate offices that share the courthouse at 116 West Miami Street in Brooksville.

Bracken County tax offices
OfficePhoneHandles
Property Valuation Administrator606-735-2228Assessment, property address, name and mailing address on the bill, exemptions
Sheriff's Office (second floor)606-735-3233Collecting this year's bill
County Clerk606-735-2952Bills from earlier years, on a separate check
  • Address or name wrong: fix it on the return stub or call the PVA.
  • Disagree with the value: call the PVA before paying.

An online portal shows bills and takes payment. Cards add a 2.50 percent charge that the cardholder pays and the sheriff does not keep. By mail, the check must cover the exact amount due.

The 2 percent discount period runs October 1 through November 1, and bills go straight to owners. The bill itself prints the later cutoffs and penalty steps, and the sheriff's office can read them to you over the phone.

Escrow causes most of the trouble. The sheriff mails the bill to the owner, never to a mortgage company. If your lender pays from escrow, pass the bill along the day it arrives, or confirm that the lender has asked the sheriff for it. A check that bounces puts the bill back to unpaid, with a returned-check fee added and the repayment schedule printed on the bill.

sections.h2: Why a bill may carry the previous owner's name
sections.html:
For tax purposes, ownership freezes on January 1. If your purchase closes after that date, the bill for the year is addressed to the person who sold. The PVA works from recorded deeds to find new owners, and a buyer whose copy never turns up can ask the sheriff for one.

As a seller, you may see a bill arrive at an address you have already left. The settlement agent normally divides the year by days of ownership and either pays the sheriff or credits whichever side will. Leave a forwarding address with the closing agent.

Book a conference at the PVA first, because state rules require one before any appeal. The roll opens to inspection for thirteen days beginning the first Monday of May. File the appeal with the clerk by the next workday after those days end.

If the PVA raises a value above what you listed, KRS 132.450(4) requires the office to notify you. Anyone paid to speak for you must be an attorney, accountant, broker, appraiser or other qualified professional, and must show your written authorization. Hearings may be recorded on audio.

sections.h2: What happens to an unpaid bill after April 15?
sections.html:
The sheriff hands every unpaid bill to the County Clerk, who records a lien and files each one as a certificate of delinquency. The clerk gives the Department of Revenue a list by May 15, and the Department publishes each county's list by June 1. On the normal schedule a tax sale can fall on any business day between July 14 and August 28.

Before that, the county attorney sends a 30-day letter and a second letter naming the sale date. The list is advertised in the paper with the biggest paid circulation between 30 and 45 days ahead, and posted online at least 30 days ahead. An owner who still owes at the sale risks having the lien assigned to an outside buyer, who may add fees.

Interest accrues at 1 percent for every month or fraction. The total grows sharply once the bill reaches the clerk, and grows again after the June advertising, so a prior-year bill should be paid as early as you can.

Owners who turn 65 during the year or are permanently disabled can claim it. The state capped the exemption at $49,100 for tax years 2025 and 2026. The house must be your owned, occupied and maintained residence on January 1, and the application is due at the PVA by December 31.

The sheriff tells eligible owners to phone the PVA before paying a bill that lacks the exemption, since the exemption shrinks the bill.

sections.h2: Paying a Bracken County bill, step by step
sections.html:
The sheriff's office collects on the second floor of the courthouse, and you have three ways to pay.

  1. In person: take the bill to the second floor at 116 West Miami Street in Brooksville.
  2. By mail: send a check that matches the amount due exactly, with the return stub, so the sheriff can apply it to the right parcel.
  3. Online: use the sheriff's portal, remembering that the 2.50 percent card charge falls on you.

Whichever route you choose, confirm the name and mailing address printed on the bill. A wrong address is the PVA's to fix, and it explains most bills that never arrive. If you have more than one parcel, check each bill separately, since the sheriff handles each one on its own.

Prior-year bills are different. They are paid to the County Clerk on a separate check, never combined with the current year's payment to the sheriff.

sections.h2: What to have ready before listing
sections.html:
A buyer's title company will look for a clean tax record, so gather the facts first. Know whether the current bill is paid and in which period. Know whether any earlier year sits at the clerk. Confirm that the name and mailing address on the bill match the deed, and ask the PVA whether a homestead exemption applies to you.

If you live in an inherited house, check the bill's owner name too. Bills follow recorded deeds, so an estate that has not recorded a transfer can leave the old owner's name on the paperwork, and the buyer's agent will ask about it.

sections.h2: How to sell a Bracken County house that owes tax
sections.html:
Treat the tax as a closing item. Get the present balance from the sheriff and any older balance from the clerk, and have the closing agent pay both from the proceeds.

  1. Call the sheriff at 606-735-3233 for this year's balance.
  2. Call the clerk at 606-735-2952 for any earlier year.
  3. Give both figures to the closing agent in writing.
  4. Ask the agent to split the current year with the buyer by days of ownership.

Inherited houses, houses with tenants and houses that need more work than a retail buyer will take on often sell to cash buyers who accept the property as it stands and pay the tax at the table.

faqs.q: What is the Bracken County PVA's phone number?
faqs.a: 606-735-2228, at the courthouse in Brooksville. The office handles assessments, mailing addresses on bills and homestead exemptions.

faqs.q: Where do I pay a Bracken County property tax bill?
faqs.a: At the sheriff's second-floor office in the courthouse, by mail, or through the sheriff's online portal. Card payments add 2.50 percent.

faqs.q: Does my mortgage company get my Bracken County tax bill?
faqs.a: No. The sheriff mails only to the owner. If your lender escrows taxes, forward the bill or ask the lender to request it.

faqs.q: Where do I pay a prior-year Bracken County bill?
faqs.a: At the County Clerk's office, 606-735-2952, with a separate check from the current year's payment.

faqs.q: Who owes tax on a Bracken County house sold in the spring?
faqs.a: The bill goes to whoever owned the house on January 1. Buyer and seller normally split the year at closing, and the agent pays the sheriff.
